extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners seeking MPEP §2106 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements integrate a judicial exception into a practical application (Alice/Mayo framework), including considerations such as 'mere instructions to apply', 'insignificant extra-solution activity', and 'field of use'. Targets Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B analyses under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception [2106.05(f)]
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more than a judicial exception (Step 2B), consider whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) or are more than mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court authority (Alice, Mayo, Benson) teaches that additional elements must do 'more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words ‘apply it’.' Claims that are nothing more than instructions to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer do not render the idea eligible. Examiners may explain why additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception. This consideration often overlaps with other §2106 considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine/conventional); those analyses may assist but the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration is evaluated only in Step 2B, not in Step 2A Prong Two. Examiners should explain on the record why limitations do not meaningfully limit the claim and refer to MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating eligibility rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (2106.05(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Recitation of claim limitations that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism is equivalent to the words 'apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are result-oriented and functional—covering any solution to an identified problem without specific steps—do not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. By contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome may integrate the exception or provide significantly more. Case examples: Electric Power Group v. Alstom (result-focused claims), Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (dynamic document/XML claims held ineligible for lacking specific steps). Examiners should analyze whether claimed steps disclose specific mechanisms rather than mere results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool (2106.05(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim invokes a computer or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (i.e., use in ordinary capacity to receive, store, or transmit data, or merely adding a general purpose computer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a computer or machinery in its ordinary capacity or adding a generic computer to an abstract idea typically does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Examples of such tool-like use include Affinity Labs v. DirecTV (cellular telephone), TLI Communications v. AV Auto (telephone and server), and Alice (intermediated settlement on a generic computer). Conversely, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology may integrate the exception (see McRO, Enfish). Examiners should compare whether the claim purports to improve technology/functionality or merely uses generic components as tools. See MPEP §§2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for improvements discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception (2106.05(f)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the particularity or generality of how the judicial exception is applied. A claim with broad applicability across many fields that generically recites an effect or claims every mode of accomplishing that effect may amount to merely adding 'apply it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that generically state a desired result or effect without limiting how it is achieved do not provide a meaningful limitation (Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). Historical examples include O’Reilly v. Morse and The Telephone Cases where overly broad claims were held ineligible. By contrast, limitations that confine the exception to a particular practical application may amount to significantly more (BASCOM example: installation of a filtering tool at a specific ISP location with customizable features). Examiners must analyze whether claim language confines the exception to a particular technological application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity [2106.05(g)]
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' includes activities incidental to the primary process or product, including pre-solution and post-solution activities (e.g., data gathering as pre-solution; printing a report as post-solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity—particularly if well-understood or conventional—does not amount to an inventive concept (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should carefully consider each claim and may use related §2106 considerations (particular machine/transformation, well-understood routine/conventional, field of use) to assist in the determination; however, the well-understood, routine, conventional analysis belongs in Step 2B, not Step 2A. If limitations are merely data gathering, selecting data sources, or trivial post-solution steps, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim and cite MPEP §2106.07(a) for rejection formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known (2106.05(g)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the extra-solution limitation is well known (token or conventional). Well-known techniques or routine activities used as add-ons are token extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case authority (Bilski; Flook; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.) shows well-known analysis techniques or use of conventional tags/techniques are token extra-solution activity. Because this overlaps with the well-understood, routine, conventional consideration, it should not be considered in the Step 2A Prong Two extra-solution activity analysis (that is evaluated in Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation is significant (2106.05(g)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that merely restrict a claim in a token way (e.g., restricting public access to media, menu ordering types) have been found insignificant (Ultramercial; Ameranth). This significance inquiry is considered in both Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should analyze whether claimed limitations meaningfully confine the judicial exception or are nominal additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting (2106.05(g)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the limitation is merely necessary data gathering and outputting—i.e., activities that all uses of the recited judicial exception require (mere inputs/outputs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures such as gathering input data, presenting offers and collecting response statistics, or verifying transactions over the Internet have been treated as mere data gathering (Mayo; OIP Technologies). This consideration is relevant in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B. Examiners should identify whether the claimed data gathering/output is intrinsic to practicing the exception and thus insignificant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity (illustrative examples from case law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples of activities courts have found to be insignificant extra-solution activity: (a) mere data gathering (clinical tests, testing system response, presenting offers and gathering statistics, verifying credit card transactions, consulting/updating logs, determining biomarker levels); (b) selecting particular data sources/types (limiting database index to XML tags; taking only certain orders); (c) insignificant application steps (cutting hair after determining hairstyle; printing/downloading generated menus); and (d) insignificant computer implementation (using conventional computer functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples (cited cases: In re Grams; In re Meyers; OIP Technologies; CyberSource; Ultramercial; Mayo; PerkinElmer; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem.; Ameranth; Electric Power Group; In re Brown; Ameranth; Fort Properties; Bancorp; In re Brown) illustrate common patterns that do not add significantly more to an exception. Use them to support explanations in eligibility rejections when limitations are merely data gathering, selection of input sources, trivial outputting, or conventional computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment [2106.05(h)]
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements merely link the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment does not make a claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook) and Federal Circuit decisions (Bilski) show that limiting an abstract idea to a particular field or adding token post-solution components does not render the concept patentable. Examiners should not permit subject matter eligibility solely because an applicant limits the claim to a particular technological environment; analyze whether the limitation meaningfully integrates the exception into a practical application rather than merely narrowing its field of use.
